name: desire for social influence
description: Wanting to have an effect on how others behave or perceive the world. This can include how they spend their money, spend their time, perceive the world, vote, etc.
perceptions: There's something I'd like others to do or know about.
I'll also benefit from helping them doing or knowing about it.

variations.name: desire to transmit knowledge
variations.description: Wanting to help others close a perceived gap in understanding. Communicating knowledge to others can legitimately help them while also helping to validate your perspective.
perceptions: Others could use help understanding something.
I know this thing well enough to help them understand it.
I may provide social value by helping them.

guidance.description: There are many references to help learn how to teach various things like academics, sports, business skills, self-improvement, etc.

variations.name: desire to persuade others
variations.description: Trying to convince others to get them to behave the way you want.
perceptions: Others are not behaving the way I think they should.
They would respond if they like me enough to try and understand my perspective.

guidance.description: Sales and negotiation skills are arts of persuading that can be useful beyond commercial purposes.

variations.name: desire to control others
variations.description: Being ready to threaten someone else's agency with negative consequences in order to get them to behave the way you want.
perceptions: Others are not behaving the way I think they should.
They won't respond to a nice approach.
There should be consequences for them not following my guidance.

guidance.description: There are parenting and workplace guides to help think about reasonable consequences.

variations.name: desire to make your mark
variations.description: Wanting to express your agency in a social context whether for the good or bad.

guidance.description: The desire to be seen is a reaction to feeling unimportant. Consider finding a way to make your mark in a positive way.

variations.name: desire to impact negatively
variations.description: Wanting to annoy or scare people from one group for revenge or to gain status with another group.
perceptions: I think negatively of some person or group.
It would be fun to see them irritated or scared.
My social group will praise me for attacking them.

guidance.description: If you're open to considering more pro-social behaviors, there are many resources online. They're probabably more boring than whatever adrenaline-soaked content got you into anti-social behavior, but they may provide a more subtle and longer lasting feeling. This doesn't suggest everyone should be nice. Just less antagonistic and more persuasive.

variations.name: desire to impact positively
perceptions: A person or group could use some help.
It could feel good to help.

guidance.description: There are many ways to volunteer in your community.

commentaries.quote: If you would persuade, you must appeal to interest rather than intellect.
Compelling reason will never convince blinding emotion.
I would rather try to persuade a man to go along, because once I have persuaded him, he will stick. If I scare him, he will stay just as long as he is scared, and then he is gone.
No act of kindness, no matter how small, is ever wasted.
commentaries.attribution: Aesop’s fable of The Lion and the Mouse

commentaries.quote: The key to successful leadership today is influence, not authority.
When marketers influence habits, they influence peoples' self-identity. And so when a group or company does something that doesn't correspond to our core values, it feels like a betrayal.
Anti-social behavior is a trait of intelligence in a world full of conformists.

People are prosocial creatures. We typically form enduring bonds with others. We find spending time with our family and friends rewarding, we rejoice in their good fortune, we want to help them and often go to a substantial degree of bother for others. This applies particularly in relation to people whom we consider to be part of our ‘in group’, but also often in relation to strangers.
